document.title: Protest of Vistra Corp. regarding PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s proposed Interim Resource Adequacy Service filing
document.group: PJM Large Load definition, Registry and Interim Resource Adequacy Service

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
 
) 
) 
) 
 
 
 
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
 
PROTEST OF VISTRA CORP. 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) submits this protest regarding 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) proposed Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) 
proposal.  Although Vistra recognizes PJM’s concerns regarding the resource adequacy challenges 
facing the region, those concerns demand durable solutions that provide investors with the 
certainty they need to maintain and expand PJM’s generation fleet.2  That is not IRAS.   
IRAS is ill-conceived, inconsistent with the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), and will stymie 
investment in PJM.  With IRAS, PJM ignores the jurisdictional boundaries that Congress carefully 
crafted and proposes rules that are unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory—each of 
which is a sufficient basis for the Commission to reject the proposal and for a court to overturn an 
order accepting IRAS on appeal.  In rejecting IRAS, the Commission should order PJM to develop 
a durable solution that is faithful to sound market fundamentals to ensure that the region has the 
capacity resources needed to meet load growth. 
 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.211. 
2 For instance, the Commission’s proposed measures to incentivize load flexibility could provide the types of 
durable solutions that bolster investor confidence, rather than undermine it.  See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 
FERC ¶ 61,211, at PP 85-87 (2026).

-2- 
Accepting IRAS would undermine the investor confidence that is critical to resource 
development because it would upset contracts negotiated in reliance on the rules in effect at the 
time.  That is a particularly concerning result now, in PJM, where the absence of predictable market 
rules in recent years has significantly undermined investment in the generation fleet needed to 
maintain resource adequacy.  If the Commission now casts doubt on the extent to which market 
participants, including both generation and load, can rely on already-executed or in-process 
bilateral contracts, it will only further impair PJM’s ability to meet its resource adequacy 
requirements at a time when the region can least afford it.3  To avoid that outcome, the Commission 
should reject IRAS altogether or clarify that new large loads that enter into contracts with existing 
capacity resources before the effective date of the IRAS reforms will not be subject to IRAS 
curtailments.   
I. 
PROTEST 
IRAS is both unlawful and counterproductive for the PJM region and the nation.  It will 
hinder investment in generation resources and data infrastructure unless and until the Commission 
rejects the proposal.  As explained below, IRAS runs afoul of the FPA in three distinct ways. 
First, as a threshold matter, IRAS oversteps the FPA’s jurisdictional boundaries because it 
targets retail customers that are outside of the Commission’s jurisdiction.  Under IRAS, PJM will 
make wholesale curtailment decisions based entirely on whether an Electric Distribution Company 
(“EDC”) has certain specific retail customers (i.e., new large loads that do utilize the Bring Your 
 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211 at P 5 (“This proceeding is not intended to disrupt existing 
commercial arrangements[.]”); FERC, Chairman Laura Swett’s Comments at PJM’s Annual Meeting in Baltimore, 
MD (May 12, 2026), https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/chairman-laura-swetts-comments-pjms-annual-
meeting-baltimore-md-0 (“[W]hatever happens, we cannot disrupt finalized commercial agreements.  At FERC, I have 
no appetite to compromise investor confidence when those investors are driving the buildout of the generation that 
PJM desperately needs.  However you get there PJM, you need to figure it out.  Fast.”).

-3- 
Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) pathway) in its footprint.  That cuts directly against Congress’s 
directive that retail service be regulated by the states, not by FERC.   
Second, IRAS is unduly discriminatory or preferential in multiple ways.4  Most glaringly, 
IRAS and BYONC unduly discriminate against existing capacity resources.  PJM proposes that 
new large loads that contract with new capacity resources are not supposed to be exposed to the 
IRAS curtailment regime while new large loads that contract with otherwise identical existing 
capacity resources would be.  This is textbook undue discrimination, as one MW of capacity from 
a new resource provides the exact same resource adequacy benefits as one MW of capacity from 
an otherwise identical existing resource.5  After all, electrons don’t differ based on the age of the 
generation facility that produced them.6  To the extent proponents of IRAS assert that these MWs 
are not identical because PJM needs one new MW of capacity for every new MW of load to solve 
its resource adequacy concerns, they are wrong for two reasons.  For one, they have not actually 
demonstrated that the system cannot handle near-term load growth—and there are good reasons to 
 
4 See, e.g., Ala. Power Co. v. FERC, 993 F.2d 1557, 1571 (D.C. Cir. 1993) (“[T]he party filing a rate adjustment 
with the Commission under § 205 bears the burden of proving the adjustment is lawful.”); ISO New England Inc., 136 
FERC ¶ 61,221, at P 20 (2011) (“Where . . . a filing is made under section 205 of the FPA, the burden of proof is on 
the filing party to show that its proposal is just and reasonable.” (footnote omitted)). 
5 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 128 FERC ¶ 61,157, at P 102 (2009) (“Both new entry and retention of existing 
efficient capacity are necessary to ensure reliability and both should receive the same price so that the price signals 
are not skewed in favor of new entry.”); see also Calpine Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,034 (2020) (Glick, Comm’r, 
Dissenting at P 84) (“[A] megawatt of capacity provided by a new resource is every bit as effective as a megawatt 
provided by an existing one.”). 
6 To underscore this point, consider how generators impact the system as a matter of physics.  Electric energy is 
“transmitted through the propagation of an electromagnetic wave;” electrons themselves do not “flow” but rather 
“oscillate in place.”  North Dakota v. Heydinger, 825 F.3d 912, 924 (8th Cir. 2016) (Murphy, J., concurring in part 
and concurring in the judgment); see also Brief of Amicus Curiae of Electrical Engineers et al., New York v. FERC, 
535 U.S. 1 (2002) (No. 00-568), 2001 WL 605124, at *7-8 (“The real energy transmission is accomplished through 
the propagation of an electromagnetic wave. Each electron is induced, under the effect of the electromagnetic wave 
generated at the power plant, to repel the electron in the next atom. Assume that energy is being transmitted left to 
right in a wire. Each electron repels its right-hand neighbor, because they are both negatively charged and similar 
charges repel each other. This ripple effect can be envisioned as each electron elbowing its neighbor toward the next 
right-hand neighboring electron, which in turn elbows the next electron, and so on down the power line. The electrons 
move very little, merely oscillating in place, but the energy – the electromagnetic wave – moves at the speed of light. 
The energized electrons making the lightbulb in a house glow are not the same electrons that were induced to oscillate 
in the generator at the generating plant.” (footnote omitted)).

-4- 
think that the system can, in fact, handle that load growth.7  For the other, they misdiagnose the 
problem: current resource adequacy concerns are caused by Load Serving Entities failing to 
procure enough capacity to cover the entirety of their load obligation, not the contracting decisions 
of individual retail customers.  And they ignore the fact that IRAS represents an unprecedented 
sea change in how customers’ service requests are viewed from a regulatory perspective.  Vistra 
is aware of no power market in history that has imposed a policy that says new customers are not 
eligible for the same service as existing customers unless they procure their own generation 
resources.8 
Third, IRAS has not been shown to be just and reasonable in several more respects.  For 
example, there is no assurance that new large loads will receive the purported benefit of BYONC 
because it is up to states and EDCs to decide curtailment orders and priorities.9  Thus, IRAS would 
impose a burden (BYONC) without any assurance that those bearing that burden would receive 
the purported benefits that are supposed to flow from it (firm service).  For that reason, IRAS is 
an illusory construct that is fundamentally unjust and unreasonable.  Further, IRAS violates cost 
causation principles, and is therefore unjust and unreasonable, because it allocates capacity costs 
to new large loads that do not bring new capacity even though it does not procure capacity to serve 
those loads.  It is also unjust and unreasonable because new large loads that do not bring new 
 
7 Ryan Hledik, Long Lam & Kate Peters, The Untapped Grid: How a Better Utilized Power System Can Improve 
Energy Affordability, The Brattle Grp., (Mar. 2026), https://www.brattle.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/The-
Untapped-Grid-Mar-2026.pdf. 
8 Vistra believes that such a policy, in addition to being unlawful, would be counterproductive for the PJM system 
because it will incentivize customers to pursue fully islanded systems to avoid system costs, thereby reducing the 
amount of load to which those costs can be spread. 
9 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service and a Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, at 92 (filed Aug. 13, 
2026) (“Transmittal”) (“[I]n recognition of the jurisdictional divide between PJM and the states and/or RERRAs, PJM 
will not direct reductions to specific New Large Loads pursuant to IRAS.  Rather, PJM is leaving it to Electric 
Distributors, in coordination with the appropriate states and/or RERRAs, LSEs, and LSE customers to determine 
which loads should ultimately reduce subject to IRAS.”).

-5- 
capacity would be subject to curtailment before demand response resources despite the fact that 
demand response resources volunteer to be curtailed and are compensated as a result.  Finally, 
IRAS is unjust and unreasonable because, by removing from the Variable Resource Reliability 
(“VRR”) Curve new large loads that do not bring new capacity, it would undermine capacity 
market fundamentals, thereby further eroding resource adequacy in PJM.  
A. IRAS Violates the FPA’s Division of Jurisdiction 
The Commission is a creature of statute and can act only within the scope of authority 
conveyed by Congress.10  IRAS exceeds the scope of the authority conveyed to the Commission 
under the FPA because the entire scheme is based on and triggered by the characteristics and 
behavior of retail customers (i.e., new large loads), which are within the states’ exclusive sphere 
to regulate.  In this way, IRAS explicitly “aims” at or “target[s]” specific retail customers, in 
violation of the FPA.11 
The FPA gives the states exclusive authority over retail sales.12  This means that the 
Commission is prohibited from specifying the rates, terms, and conditions of retail sales “no matter 
how direct, or dramatic, [their] impact on wholesale rates” as that “is a job for the States alone.”13  
Nevertheless, “[w]holesale and retail markets in electricity . . . are not hermetically sealed from 
each other,” so to determine whether an action that affects both wholesale and retail spheres 
oversteps the FPA’s bright jurisdictional line, the Supreme Court has considered “the target at 
 
10 Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 8 (D.C. Cir. 2002). 
11 FERC v. Elect. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 282 (“EPSA”) (quoting Oneok, Inc. v. Learjet Inc., 575 U.S. 
373, 385 (2015) (“Oneok”))). 
12 16 U.S.C. § 824(b); Niagara Mohawk Power Corp. v. FERC, 452 F.3d 822, 824 (D.C. Cir. 2006) (“Under 
section 201(b)(1) of the Federal Power Act, 16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1), FERC has jurisdiction over both the interstate 
transmission of electricity and the sale of electricity at wholesale in interstate commerce. States retain jurisdiction 
over retail sales of electricity and over local distribution facilities.”). 
13 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 279-80.

-6- 
which [a] law aims.”14  FERC cannot approve a proposal where retail customers are the “target at 
which [the proposal] aims.”15 
That is IRAS to a T.  Under IRAS, PJM decides which wholesale transmission customers 
are subject to curtailment based on the characteristics of individual retail customers—that is the 
central feature of IRAS.16  Specifically, PJM will curtail EDCs with new large loads (i.e., retail 
customers) in their footprints that do not bring sufficient new capacity to offset their demand.17  
That makes IRAS all about the retail customer: when it comes online (before or after June 1, 2027), 
its size (more or less than 50 MW), and whether it brings offsetting new capacity (i.e., BYONC).18   
Under IRAS, retail customers and their characteristics are far more than “the mechanism through 
which [IRAS] operates,”19 they are lynchpin of the entire scheme and the determining factor for 
whether IRAS applies.  Moreover, PJM is clear, again and again, that the purpose of IRAS is to 
shape the behavior of retail customers and to “solve” the resource adequacy challenge that PJM 
posits, a task that should be reserved for the PJM capacity market.20 
 
14 Id. at 282 (quoting Oneok, 575 U.S. at 385) (alterations in original). 
15 Oneok, 575 U.S. at 385. 
16 See, e.g., Transmittal at 85-86. 
17 Id. at 83-84. 
18 Id. at 6, 86; see also id. at 1 n.2 (proposing to define “New Large Load” as: either: (a) a Large Load that goes 
into service after June 1, 2027, or (b) incremental load in-service after June 1, 2027, that increases the existing end-
use customer load at a single electrical site that, prior to such incremental load, did not previously meet the definition 
of Large Load; id. at 32-33 (proposing to define Large Load as a load that (1) has a peak load of 50 MW or greater; 
(2) is located at a single site; and (3) is behind one or more points of interconnection.”); id. at 69 (“All New Large 
Loads shall be eligible to provide IRAS and considered Eligible New Large Loads to the extent the combination of 
their BYONC arrangements and Allocated RBP UCAP MW does not meet their capacity needs.”).   
19 EPSA. 577 U.S. at 283. 
20 See, e.g., Transmittal at 7 (“IRAS would facilitate a decision by an Electric Distributor in conjunction with 
relevant state entities, as applicable, to decide that specific Eligible New Large Loads may be reduced during a 
Delivery Year when IRAS applies, because such loads are not arranged with sufficient new capacity.”); id. at 50 (“To 
incentivize Large Loads to address the capacity shortfall caused by their rapid growth, in both speed to interconnection 
and volume of capacity needed, PJM is proposing to allow New Large Loads to remove themselves—in whole or in 
part—from the MW eligible for IRAS where such loads bring new capacity to the PJM Region.”); id. at 124 (“The

-7- 
Contrast IRAS with the Supreme Court’s decision in EPSA, where the Court upheld Order 
No. 745 because (i) it did not literally regulate retail rates and (ii) the regulation did not target the 
retail customer.21  There, the demand response rule was “only about[] improving the wholesale 
market,” and FERC “focused wholly on the benefits that demand response participation (in the 
wholesale market) could bring to the wholesale market.”22  Any effects on the retail market were 
incidental at most and beside the point.  The same cannot be said of IRAS, which, as noted, is all 
about specific retail loads and tailoring wholesale services to address the decisions and actions of 
those retail loads.  Whereas EPSA upheld a FERC decision that accommodated retail customers 
by requiring RTOs/ISOs to enable them—if permitted by their state—to participate in FERC-
jurisdictional wholesale markets through a FERC-jurisdictional product, IRAS would, through 
EDCs, regulate the nature and conditions of service that retail customers receive.   
It is obvious from how IRAS operates that PJM is targeting retail customers.  Recall that 
PJM proposes to assign wholesale curtailment obligation to an EDC based on the size (i.e., more 
than 50 MW) and vintage (i.e., interconnection date and ramp rate) of the relevant retail 
customers.23  PJM’s characterization of IRAS confirms the target, despite its veneer of regulating 
EDCs rather than retail load.  First, the PJM board directed PJM to file a proposal that “will be 
applicable to ‘[N]ew Large Loads that, as of June 1, 2027, do not bring sufficient capacity to serve 
their resource adequacy needs and cannot otherwise be served at the 1-in-10 reliability 
 
elements of this proposal were developed together and designed to work in lockstep and provide complementary 
pieces to a multi-prong approach to incent New Large Loads to bring their own capacity to meet their resource 
adequacy needs and avoid imposing costs on ratepayers.”). 
21 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282-83.   
22 Id. at 282-83. 
23 Transmittal at 6.

-8- 
standard.’”24  Next, PJM defined IRAS as “a new supplemental capacity product through which 
New Large Loads provide a load reduction service that is a tool available to PJM to manage 
resource adequacy shortfalls.”25  At every turn, PJM has made clear that it designed IRAS as a 
way to curtail specific retail customers.  That these curtailments would be carried out by EDCs 
does not change the fact that the trigger for the curtailments is the characteristics of the retail 
customer—or that the curtailment directive is pursuant to a FERC-jurisdictional tariff.  Indeed, 
that type of formalistic argument is why the Supreme Court has repeatedly emphasized the target 
at which the regulation aims.26  Finally, as yet another piece of evidence, the wholesale 
transmission curtailments will mirror “a MW quantity equal to or less than the Electric 
Distributor’s Eligible New Large Load.”27  In other words, PJM plans to call for curtailments not 
based on the real-time transmission conditions in an EDC’s zone, which is how PJM sheds loads 
today, but based on whether a zone has retail customers that have certain characteristics.  It is easy 
to see that this is not a regulation where “every aspect of the regulatory plan happens exclusively 
on the wholesale market and governs exclusively that market’s rules.”28 
In trying to defend IRAS as jurisdictionally permissible, PJM hangs its hat on the fact that 
“‘exclusive jurisdiction’ rests with the states to ensure that the appropriate retail customers, i.e., 
New Large Loads, including data centers—and not residential customers or small industrial 
 
24 Transmittal at 17 (alteration in original). 
25 Id. at 22. 
26 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282 (looking at the Commission’s justification for regulating demand response and quoting 
from the Court’s decision in Oneok, which “consider[ed] ‘the target at which [a] law aims’ in determining whether a 
State [was] properly regulating retail or, instead, improperly regulating wholesale sales.” (quoting Oneok, 575 U.S. at 
385) (emphasis and alteration in original)); cf. Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 166 (2016) (state’s 
scheme to encourage development of generation resources overstepped its authority because it was tethered to the 
resource’s wholesale market participation).   
27 Transmittal at 86. 
28 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282.

-9- 
customers—are reduced when system conditions call for PJM to require load reductions,”29 but 
the fact that PJM is not the party that physically “flips the switch” to curtail specific retail loads 
does not save IRAS.  Creating the conditions by which a state must take the final step of curtailing 
retail customers that PJM has already singled out for curtailment does not retroactively cure the 
jurisdictional defects inherent in IRAS.    
IRAS also exceeds the Commission’s authority for the related reason that PJM seeks to 
regulate retail customers and their rates—albeit indirectly—which the FPA and EPSA prohibit.  It 
bears repeating that the Commission cannot regulate retail customers, even indirectly, in ways that 
target the retail customer.30  But that is IRAS in a nutshell.  The whole point of IRAS is to have 
certain retail loads curtailed under PJM-defined conditions.31  Deciding when certain large loads 
should be curtailed is a condition of retail distribution service, not something to be decided by an 
RTO, as PJM would be doing here.   
PJM also proposes to overstep its jurisdictional limits by setting forth how retail customers 
are compensated when they are curtailed under IRAS.32  Under IRAS, PJM would compensate 
EDCs for IRAS curtailments at a rate that is equal to 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate.33  
Specifically, PJM proposes to pay a wholesale rate to EDCs that curtail under IRAS, but if a new 
large load waives curtailment compensation at the retail level, the wholesale IRAS rate will be 
 
29 Transmittal at 90-91. 
30 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282-83.   
31 See Transmittal at 22 (defining IRAS as “a new supplemental capacity product through which New Large Loads 
provide a load reduction service that is a tool available to PJM to manage resource adequacy shortfalls.”). 
32 PJM indicates that the ultimate wholesale rate for IRAS would not be reviewed under FPA section 205.  See 
id. at 102.  To the extent that PJM is proposing to charge rates that differ from what is on file with the Commission, 
this would violate the filed rate doctrine.  
33 Id.

-10- 
reduced to zero dollars.34  In other words, PJM is creating a mechanism within the wholesale rate 
that determines retail compensation, namely the waiver election on the part of the new large load, 
which controls whether a payment is made to an end-use customer.  That is a direct regulation of 
the retail customer.    
Thus, IRAS regulates the retail customer, which is why it differs from other issues 
involving large loads that lie at the confluence of federal and state jurisdiction.  For example, in 
the PJM Large Load Order to Show Cause,35 the Commission has asserted jurisdiction over 
discrete aspects of the interconnection of large loads to the transmission system based on the 
Commission’s jurisdiction over the interstate transmission of electricity.  That regulation does not 
come close to touching the ultimate sale of electricity to the retail customer, whereas IRAS directly 
regulates it.  Instead, the Large Load Order to Show Cause is all about “ensur[ing] that transmission 
provider and/or transmission owner tariffs include sufficiently clear and consistent provisions 
governing how transmission service to Eligible Customers”—i.e., the entity taking wholesale 
transmission service—“on behalf of large loads interconnecting to the transmission system will be 
studied.”36  To the extent that the regulation affects retail customers, such effects are incidental to 
the purpose of the Large Load Order to Show Cause.  Further, as Vistra has previously explained, 
the Commission’s jurisdiction over the transmission of electricity in interstate commerce—the 
basis for Commission action in the Large Load Order to Show Cause—is plenary and therefore 
broader than its jurisdiction with respect to sales wholesale sales of electricity—the basis for IRAS, 
 
34 Id. at 105; Proposed Tariff, attach. DD-4, § X(a) (“The rate for the provision of Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service shall be 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate specified in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 10A(e), unless 
any Eligible New Large Load elects to (i) accept in its retail rates a sum less than 50% of the Non-Performance Charge 
Rate as compensation for the provision of wholesale Interim Resource Adequacy Service, or (ii) waive receipt in its 
retail rates any compensation for the provision of wholesale Interim Resource Adequacy Service . . . . ”). 
35 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211.  
36 Id. P 45 (emphasis added).

-11- 
which operates through PJM’s wholesale capacity market and is all about the supply of electricity 
in the region.37   
B. IRAS Is Unduly Discriminatory 
IRAS is also unduly discriminatory because it treats similarly situated entities differently.38  
“Similarly situated” does not mean that there are no differences between the two entities, but rather 
that there are no differences “that are material to the inquiry at hand.”39  PJM bears the burden to 
explain how its proposal to treat entities differently is justified by factors that render those entities 
not “similarly situated.”  PJM fails to meet that standard for several reasons. 
1. IRAS Unduly Discriminates Between EDCs 
To start, IRAS would unduly discriminate among EDCs based on the characteristics of 
retail customers within those EDCs’ footprints.  Specifically, IRAS would subject EDCs to 
curtailment based on the size, timing, and contracting decisions of its retail customers.  Those retail 
customers are outside the Commission’s jurisdiction to consider and therefore cannot be “material 
to the inquiry at hand.”40  Providing differing levels of wholesale market treatment depending on 
legally irrelevant characteristics of entities sitting outside the Commission’s jurisdiction is, by 
definition, unduly discriminatory.   
Even if the characteristics of the retail customers within an EDC’s territory could, in theory, 
be a lawful basis to discriminate among wholesale customers, the retail characteristics on which 
 
37 See Interconnection of Large Loads to the Transmission Sys., Docket No. RM26-4-000, Initial Comments of 
Vistra Corp., at 7 (filed Nov. 21, 2025). 
38 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b); see also Transmission Agency of N. California v. FERC, 628 F.3d 538, 551 (D.C. Cir. 
2010) (citing Sacramento Mun. Util. Dist. v. FERC, 474 F.3d 797, 802 (D.C. Cir. 2007)). 
39 See N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 162 FERC ¶ 61,124, at PP 10, 14 (2018) (“To say that entities are similarly 
situated does not mean that there are no differences between them; rather, it means that there are no differences that 
are material to the inquiry at hand”); see also Ala. Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 684 F.2d 20, 27 (D.C. Cir. 1982) (explaining 
that if the costs of providing service to two groups are different, the two classes are differently situated in that 
“important respect” for cost-of-service ratemaking). 
40 N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 162 FERC ¶ 61,124 at P 10.

-12- 
PJM proposes to discriminate are irrelevant to the resource adequacy issues that IRAS purports to 
solve, and therefore do not render the EDCs differently situated.  PJM has misdiagnosed the cause 
of the resource adequacy problem.  The regional resource adequacy problem is not caused by the 
individual contracting decisions of each retail customer.  The resource adequacy problem is that 
some EDCs have agreed to serve more load than they have generation.  Were PJM to continue to 
assign load shed to EDCs that are short, it is likely that EDCs that interconnect large loads without 
the generation to serve it would be exposed to curtailment.  The current method aims at generation 
deficient zones, with the potential they are short due to additional large loads.  PJM skips past the 
question of whether an EDC is generation deficient and aims simply at EDCs that have large loads 
that do not bring their own new capacity.   
2. IRAS Unduly Discriminates Against Existing Resources 
When determining whether new large loads are subject to IRAS, PJM would value identical 
new and existing capacity resources differently even though they provide the same resource 
adequacy benefits to the system.  PJM has not explained why large loads that contract with new 
generation resources should be non-curtailable while those that contract with existing generation 
resource with the same capacity value should be curtailed when system conditions warrant.  Nor 
could it.  One MW of accredited capacity from a new resource provides the same resource 
adequacy benefits as one MW of capacity from an otherwise identical existing resource.  Whether 
the otherwise identical resources are bilaterally contracted or selling exclusively in the PJM 
capacity market does not change the resource adequacy value to the PJM system as a matter of 
physics. 
Indeed, the D.C. Circuit has held that is arbitrary and capricious for the Commission to 
treat new and existing customers differently where both contribute equally to the need in

-13- 
question.41  So too, the Commission has previously rejected efforts by PJM to treat new and 
existing capacity resources differently, even when the avowed purpose was to incentivize new 
resource entry.42  In that case, PJM proposed to lock in capacity prices for new capacity resources 
for seven years, which would guarantee higher prices to new entrants that were not available to 
existing suppliers.  The Commission rejected the proposal, explaining that both new and existing 
capacity are necessary to ensure reliability and that both should receive the same price so that the 
price signals are not skewed in favor of new entry.43  That logic applies with force here because 
IRAS gives preferential treatment to one MW of new capacity even though one MW of existing 
capacity is equally as effective when it comes to ensuring resource adequacy. 
3. IRAS Unduly Discriminates Based on Vintage of Load Addition 
Next, IRAS also unduly discriminates between new and existing large loads given that 
curtailment obligations would be assigned to the EDC based on when the large loads in question 
began operating, a characteristic that is entirely irrelevant to reliability and resource adequacy 
concerns.  As already discussed, the D.C. Circuit has rejected similar efforts to treat existing and 
marginal customers differently based on the principal that, because every user of a system is 
economically marginal, increases in demand can be attributed to every user, both new and 
existing.44  That principle forecloses IRAS, which would treat EDCs with large loads that begin 
operations on May 31, 2027 differently than those with large loads that begin operations the next 
 
41 See BNP Paribas Energy Trading GP v. FERC, 743 F.3d 264, 268 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (“[T]he cost causation 
principle generally calls for giving the same treatment to new and continuing customers, based on a straightforward 
economic rationale.  Where ‘all customers cause the incurrence of the costs . . . , whether by adding or merely 
continuing their usage assignment of the costs to all customers (both continuing and new) forces each set to weigh the 
marginal benefits of the capacity to them against the marginal costs they impose on society by continuing to make 
demands.” (internal citations and quotation marks omitted)). 
42 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 128 FERC ¶ 61,157 at PP 101-102. 
43 Id.; see also id. P 103 (“A market should be designed correctly so that the contribution to reliability from both 
new entrants and existing suppliers is compensated comparably.”). 
44 See BNP Paribas Energy Trading GP v. FERC, 743 F.3d at 268-69.

-14- 
day, even though it is the load’s size, not the date that it started operating, that determines its effect 
on resource adequacy. 
PJM’s proposal to reset the IRAS curtailment regime if the region has sufficient capacity 
to meet the reliability requirement for three consecutive delivery years further underscores the 
unduly discriminatory nature of IRAS.  Consider a hypothetical in which a new large load is 
subject to IRAS for the first two years it is in operation, after which the resource adequacy picture 
in the region improves for three years and there are no shortfalls during that time.  At that point—
five years after it began operating—the new large load would no longer be subject to IRAS 
curtailments going forward even if a shortfall returns in year six.45  But a new load coming online 
in year six that does not BYONC would be subject to curtailment.  Toggling IRAS’s curtailment 
scheme in this way makes no sense, as the demand that the large load puts on PJM’s system (i.e., 
its effect on resource adequacy) remains constant in all six years.  As this example shows, IRAS 
would subject large loads to discriminatory treatment based solely on the resource adequacy 
picture in PJM at the time those loads begin operating rather than on the loads’ effects on resource 
adequacy—a principle that is inconsistent with the D.C. Circuit’s BNP Paribas decision.46   
C. IRAS Is Unjust and Unreasonable 
IRAS is unjust and unreasonable for at least five reasons.  First, it is designed to require 
new large loads to bring new capacity to avoid being curtailed even though PJM lacks the authority 
to ensure that such loads will not, in fact, be curtailed.  Second, under IRAS, new large loads that 
do not bring new capacity are allocated costs for capacity that PJM never procures.  Third, IRAS 
 
45 Transmittal at 58. 
46 Even if the Commission were to order PJM to apply IRAS and BYONC to a wider range of large loads (putting 
aside the filed-rate doctrine issues this would raise), any scheme in which preferential treatment would turn on the 
vintage of loads in an EDC’s footprint would be patently illegal, as the D.C. Circuit has made clear.  BNP Paribas 
Energy Trading GP v. FERC, 743 F.3d at 268-69.

-15- 
fails to respect existing contracts because new large loads that contract with existing capacity 
resources prior to the effective date of IRAS are nevertheless subject to the IRAS curtailment 
regime.  Fourth, it curtails loads seeking firm service before those that have volunteered to be 
curtailed.  Finally, PJM’s proposal to remove from the VRR Curve large loads that do not bring 
their own capacity distorts market fundamentals and could lock in any resource adequacy gap that 
remains after the backstop auction.  Each of these flaws is a sufficient basis to reject the filing.   
1. IRAS Does Not Ensure That BYONC Loads Get the Benefit of the 
Bargain 
IRAS is unjust and unreasonable because it imposes costs on new large loads without 
commensurate benefits.  As PJM implicitly concedes, new large loads that that seek to acquire 
firm service via BYONC could still be curtailed under IRAS before pre-emergency load 
management reductions.47  To see why, recall how IRAS is designed to work.  When called upon 
by PJM, an EDC must curtail load in an amount equal to the sum of Eligible New Large Load 
Amounts in the EDC’s footprint—i.e., the sum of new large loads that do not BYONC.48  A new 
large load that brings sufficient new capacity to offset its demand is not considered eligible to be 
curtailed under IRAS.49  Nevertheless, as PJM itself concedes, “while PJM will determine the 
quantity of MW that load in a zone/area will need to be reduced by to maintain system reliability 
in the PJM Region, states may determine—under their own laws, policies, and definition of what 
constitutes ‘large load’—which resources will be called on to reduce load.”50   
 
47 See Transmittal at 92 (“PJM will not direct reductions to specific New Large Loads pursuant to IRAS.  Rather, 
PJM is leaving it to Electric Distributors, in coordination with the appropriate states and/or RERRAs, LSEs, and LSE 
customers to determine which loads should ultimately reduce subject to IRAS.”). 
48 Id.at 71-72. 
49 Id. at 69.  
50 Id. at 87.

-16- 
This means that even though BYONC large loads are not considered eligible for 
curtailment by PJM, EDCs will decide which loads to shed according to retail tariffs and state 
policy priorities, which could include BYONC large loads.  In other words, PJM has designed a 
scheme in which it purports to protect certain loads from being curtailed, even though PJM has no 
way to ensure that those loads are not, in fact, curtailed.  As a result, new large loads that spend 
billions of dollars contracting with new capacity resources may be curtailed before ones that do 
not bring new capacity because PJM has no authority to determine which retail customers to shed.  
The fact that the ultimate curtailment decision is a retail question does not excuse this result.  The 
Commission must determine whether the construct proposed by PJM is just and reasonable—a 
conclusion it cannot make for a program, like IRAS, that creates a burden but does not deliver the 
benefit that it is purportedly premised on. 
2. IRAS Is Unjust and Unreasonable Because It Allocates RPM Costs to 
Loads for Capacity that They Never Procure 
IRAS is also unjust and unreasonable because it flagrantly violates bedrock cost causation 
and beneficiary pays principles.  Under IRAS, PJM would exclude from the VRR Curve new large 
loads that fail to bring new capacity while still allocating capacity charges to them.51  By design, 
PJM’s proposal would meddle with capacity market fundamentals to avoid procuring capacity to 
serve new large loads that fail to bring new capacity and yet turn around and allocate capacity 
costs to those very same loads.  This scheme is inconsistent with the requirement that costs 
assigned to a party must be “roughly commensurate” with the benefit it receives in exchange for 
 
51 See Proposed Tariff, attach. DD, § 5.10(a) (deducting Excluded New Large Load Amounts from the Reliability 
Requirement used to establish the VRR Curve).  PJM does not propose to change how it calculates and allocates 
capacity charges.

-17- 
paying those costs.52  It would be impossible for new large loads to get a benefit from capacity 
they are paying for when that capacity is never acquired for them in the first place. 
As discussed further below,53 this aspect of PJM’s proposal is not just unlawful, it is also 
dangerously short-sighted as a matter of policy.  In the short term, administratively suppressing 
demand in the capacity market might help insulate existing retail customers from price increases 
due to large loads. But it is not a lasting solution.  Instead, by removing from the VRR Curve loads 
that will come online in the region, PJM is further eroding capacity market fundamentals, which 
will undermine investment in the region’s generation fleet, thereby harming resource adequacy in 
the long-term and ultimately increasing costs for the region.   
3. IRAS Is Unjust and Unreasonable Because It Disrupts Existing 
Commercial Arrangements 
Furthermore, IRAS is unjust and unreasonable because it fails to respect existing contracts.  
Specifically, new large loads that contract with existing capacity resources prior to the effective 
date of IRAS will be subject to the IRAS curtailment regime.  Despite PJM’s claim that its proposal 
will not disrupt existing contracts, IRAS will force large loads that have already paid for capacity 
by contracting with existing generation to pay for capacity price twice by BYONC to try to avoid 
curtailment.  Requiring an entity to pay twice for the same product or service is unjust and 
unreasonable.54  
Subjecting new large loads that have executed contracts with existing generators to IRAS 
will disrupt settled expectations and compound uncertainty in the PJM region, chilling investment 
in energy infrastructure when it is most needed.  Some new loads that will not come online until 
 
52 See Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1256 (D.C. Cir. 2018). 
53 See Infra § I.C.5. 
54 See N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 155 FERC ¶ 61,076, at P 82 (2016) (rejecting proposal that would have 
required ratepayers to pay twice for the same capacity).

-18- 
after June 1, 2027 have already entered into bilateral contracts to purchase capacity from existing 
generators or are currently in the process of negotiating such contracts that will be executed prior 
to the IRAS effective date.  If those contracts are not honored, the Commission and PJM will only 
reinforce investors’ fears that the ground in PJM can shift beneath them at any point.  That will 
throttle investment into the region and jeopardize resource adequacy.  
For example, Vistra previously entered into power purchase agreements for the sale of 
nuclear power from Vistra’s operating nuclear facilities in Ohio with a data center customer.55  As 
proposed, IRAS would not extend curtailment protection to capacity procured under agreements 
of this kind, notwithstanding that these agreements were executed prior to the effectiveness of 
IRAS.  That result would create the prospect of duplicative capacity procurement and would 
unsettle the expectations of underlying agreements that were negotiated within the existing 
regulatory framework.  The Commission must not adopt IRAS in a form that operates retroactively 
on existing agreements. 
Even if the Commission were otherwise inclined to accept IRAS, it must reject the proposal 
solely for its failure to exempt contracts with existing resources.  In so doing, the Commission 
should provide guidance that, in any future filing, PJM must grandfather contracts between new 
large loads and existing capacity resources negotiated according to the rules in effect at the time.  
This would be consistent with PJM’s own statement and FERC’s approach to honoring existing 
contracts and reliance interests.56  Without such grandfathering, new large loads will have paid 
 
55 Vistra, Vistra and Meta Announce Agreements to Support Nuclear Plants in PJM and Add New Nuclear 
Generation to the Grid (Jan. 9, 2026), https://investor.vistracorp.com/2026-01-09-Vistra-and-Meta-Announce-
Agreements-to-Support-Nuclear-Plants-in-PJM-and-Add-New-Nuclear-Generation-to-the-Grid.  
56 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at PP 222-224 (2025); N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, 
Inc., 122 FERC ¶ 61,267, at P 65 (2008); ISO New England Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,249, at P 34 (2026); see also FERC, 
Chairman Laura Swett’s Comments at PJM’s Annual Meeting in Baltimore, MD (May 12, 2026),

-19- 
billions of dollars for capacity only to then be subjected to curtailment risk and double-charged for 
capacity from the PJM market which they do not need.  That type of regulatory framework is a 
sure recipe for scaring off investment not only in PJM but any market regulated by FERC that 
might follow PJM’s lead.    
4. IRAS Is Unjust and Unreasonable Because it Creates a Scheme to Curtail 
Loads Seeking Firm Service Before Those That Volunteer to Be 
Curtailable 
Further, under IRAS’s tortured curtailment scheme, new large loads that are seeking firm 
service could be curtailed before loads that have volunteered to participate as demand response 
resources.  PJM proposes to call for an IRAS curtailment “prior to calling on Pre-Emergency Load 
Management Reduction Actions” when it determines that system conditions warrant such action.57  
In practice, this means that new large loads that depend on firm service to operate but have not 
brought new capacity for any number of reasons (e.g., because the paired generation cannot clear 
the backlogged interconnection queue) could be curtailed before loads that have elected to be 
curtailed whenever called upon by PJM to do so.  And to make matters worse, demand response 
resources will receive capacity payments and be curtailed after new large loads subject to IRAS.  
Curtailing loads that have paid for firm service before those that have raised their hand to be 
curtailable is unjust and unreasonable.   
5. IRAS Will Undermine PJM’s Capacity Market Fundamentals, Which 
Will Further Harm Resource Adequacy in PJM  
IRAS’s design flaws are also unjust and unreasonable because they will deter investment 
needed to bolster resource adequacy in the region at a time when that investment is desperately 
 
https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/chairman-laura-swetts-comments-pjms-annual-meeting-baltimore-md-0 
(“[W]hatever happens, we cannot disrupt finalized commercial agreements.  At FERC, I have no appetite to 
compromise investor confidence when those investors are driving the buildout of the generation that PJM desperately 
needs.  However you get there PJM, you need to figure it out.  Fast.”). 
57 Transmittal at 75.

-20- 
needed.  PJM asserts that it is proposing to remove large load that does not BYONC from the 
demand curve to protect other customers from high costs.58  This is counterproductive because it 
will lock in any reliability gap that exists after the reliability backstop auction is run.   
Dr. Carl Coscia’s affidavit on behalf of P3 illustrates the sensitivity of the capacity price 
when load is removed from the capacity market.59  When demand growth is removed from the 
auction, even a modest amount of resource entry will drive the capacity price below the cost of 
new entry.60  Consistent and predictable demand growth can mitigate the disincentive to enter 
based on a single year’s capacity price because entry is less likely to reduce future capacity prices 
below the level that made the entry rational.  Thus, PJM’s proposal to remove load growth 
associated with large loads that do not BYONC will likely disincentivize the entry needed to close 
any reliability gap remaining after the backstop auction. 
With the capacity market less able to attract entry based on PJM’s proposal, one is left to 
question what will motivate new entry.  PJM seems to be relying on the BYONC elements of its 
proposal.  As discussed above, IRAS leaves large loads in an impossible situation:  they can either 
contract with new capacity with nothing more than the hope that the state will honor BYONC, 
such that they will not be curtailed; or they can forgo BYONC, and hope that they are not curtailed, 
either because system conditions never warrant it or because states decide to curtail other loads 
first.  Further, removing load growth from the demand curve deepens the conundrum for any large 
load considering a costly bilateral contract for capacity.  While PJM’s proposal will likely 
disincentivize new generation, there remains a chance that enough new resources will enter so that 
 
58 Transmittal at 109-119. 
59 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. Protest of PJM Power Providers (P3) Group, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Aff. of 
Dr. Carl Coscia (to be filed Sep. 3, 2026).  P3 has informed Vistra that they intend to attach the affidavit of Dr. Coscia 
and has authorized us to represent that here.  
60 Id.

-21- 
capacity prices will drop significantly.  A new large load that is not fully protected from IRAS 
curtailment must weigh the certainty of costly new generation against the chance for significantly 
less costly capacity.  PJM is asking large loads to take a gamble.  Under those circumstances, it 
would be entirely rational and predictable if new large loads choose the side of the wager that does 
not involve them making a potentially multi-billion-dollar commitment.  In practice, that means 
an exodus of capital from the region, or a flight to fully islanded configurations, which would be 
contrary to the stated goals of IRAS and the best interests of all PJM stakeholders. 
In short, PJM’s proposal will likely either disincentivize new entry into the PJM capacity 
market but encourage BYONC, thus locking in whatever reliability gap remains after PJM’s 
planned Reliability Backstop Procurement auction; or it will encourage new entry through the 
capacity market and discourage BYONC, thereby creating a permanent class of load subject to 
IRAS curtailment and driving capital away from the region.  Either result will work against the 
region’s needs, so whichever way the IRAS gamble plays out it is clear that the end state will harm 
PJM customers. 
D. IRAS Should Not Apply to Behind the Meter Load 
Finally, the Commission should require PJM to confirm that IRAS will not apply to new 
large loads that are co-located behind the meter of generation resources that are not capacity 
resources.  For loads in such a configuration, there is nothing to curtail because the load is not 
using PJM capacity.  The Commission must direct PJM to provide this confirmation to ensure that 
this proceeding does not undermine the Commission’s parallel efforts to facilitate co-location. 
PJM’s filing introduces significant ambiguity about whether it intends to subject co-located 
loads to IRAS because it deviates from the Commission’s proposed definitions concerning co-
located configurations in the PJM Large Load Order to Show Cause in Docket No. EL26-67-000.  
There, the Commission defined a “large load” as “a new, commercial or industrial customer,

-22- 
located at a single site behind one or more points of interconnection, and that has a peak load of 
50 MW or greater, interconnects to the transmission system at a voltage level of greater than 69 
kV, and is not part of a co-location arrangement.”61  To contrast, PJM’s proposed definitions for 
“Large Load” and “New Large Load” specifically do not exclude load that is part of a co-location 
arrangement.62  PJM’s decision not to carve out co-located load in the manner the Commission 
intended indicates that co-located loads could be subject to IRAS.   
PJM did not and cannot explain why IRAS should apply to co-located loads.  Instead, PJM 
attempted to justify its inclusion of co-located load in these definitions by stating that it “proposed 
rules that specifically address situations in which Large Load is co-located with their own 
generation.”63 It is not clear what rules PJM is referring to, as nothing in PJM’s proposal clarifies 
how IRAS will work for co-located load.64   
It would be manifestly unjust and unreasonable to curtail a load that is co-located behind 
the meter of a generator that is not a capacity resource.  If PJM, in conjunction with EDCs, were 
to seek to curtail a new large load co-located with a non-capacity resource, it would need to direct 
the co-located generator to increase output to the grid because the co-located load is not a network 
load subject to EDC direction.  But the co-located generator is not paid to be a capacity resource 
so PJM has no claim to the generator’s output.  Further, the co-located generator may no longer be 
deliverable to all load as it is required to forfeit its capacity injection rights, and so it may not be 
 
61 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 195 FERC ¶ 61,211 at P 58 (emphasis added). 
62 Transmittal at 31, 35-36, 38.  PJM’s proposed definition also fails to include a voltage threshold.  PJM also 
fails to justify this omission, stating only that its stakeholders “have not identified any need” to include a voltage 
threshold.  Id. at 36.  That is not a sufficient reason to ignore a Commission directive. 
63 Id. 
64 For example, because a co-located load is behind a generator’s point of interconnection, the only way to curtail 
that load may be to disconnect the generator.  Such an action would raise serious legal and operational issues—for 
both the generator, the load, and the PJM system—and ultimately would be counterproductive from a resource 
adequacy perspective.

-23- 
able to improve system conditions.  PJM has not, and cannot, justify including co-located new 
large loads in IRAS.  Accordingly, the Commission should order PJM to confirm that such loads 
are not subject to IRAS curtailments. 
II. 
 CONCLUSION 
For the foregoing reasons, the Commission should promptly reject PJM’s filing.
